title: The script and the vowel points

objectives.can: Read Aramaic words in the square script with their vowel points, from right to left.

explanation.summary: Biblical Aramaic is written in the same square script as the Hebrew Bible, from right to left, and the Masoretes pointed it with the same vowel signs. Learn the twenty-two letters, the five final forms and the vowel points, and every Aramaic word in this course becomes readable.

sections.heading: One script, read from right to left
body: The Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra is printed in the square script that most readers know from the Hebrew Bible. A line begins at its right-hand edge and is read toward the left; so is every word. When you look at a verse such as Daniel 2:4, find the right-hand end of the line first. The first word the library holds for that verse is the word for 'the king', and it is the right-most word.

There are no capital letters, and the words are separated by spaces. The script is itself an Aramaic inheritance: it is generally held to have developed from the alphabet that Aramaic scribes used across the Persian empire, and Jewish scribes came to prefer it for writing Hebrew as well. That is why the 'Hebrew' letters you may already know are also the letters of Aramaic.

In this library the Aramaic stands in Daniel 2 to 7 and Ezra 4 to 7, with one verse of Jeremiah and two words of Genesis. Together they are about 4,800 words. The course teaches only what these words show.

sections.heading: Twenty-two letters
body: The first table lists the twenty-two letters in alphabetical order, with the name each has, the usual way of writing it in Latin letters (its transliteration), and two columns of sound. The letters are all consonants, though four of them (alef, he, vav and yod) can also help to show a vowel; lesson A0.1.2 explains how.

The two sound columns are two conventions. 'Modern' is the pronunciation of Israeli Hebrew, which many courses use because it is easy to learn and to hear. 'Tiberian' is a reconstruction of the careful reading tradition of the Masoretes, the scholars of Tiberias who gave the Bible its vowel points and accents. Neither is a recording of how Aramaic sounded in the time of Daniel or Ezra. Use whichever your teacher or tradition prefers. The spelling never changes.
Learn each letter by its shape, not by its transliteration. A reader sees the word for 'dream' as four letters, not as a sequence of Latin letters.

sections.heading: Final forms and look-alike letters
body: Five letters (kaf, mem, nun, pe and tsade) have a different shape when they end a word. The second table shows them. A final nun is the one that most often causes trouble because it looks like a long vav, and the final form of the plural ending in Aramaic nouns is the nun of the common ending -ין.

Several letters look alike. The third table lists the pairs that beginners confuse: bet and kaf, dalet and resh, he, het and tav, vav and final nun, and a few others. In a printed Bible the strokes are small, so slow looking at the actual letter, not at the word as a whole, is the cure.

sections.heading: The vowel points
body: Vowels are written as small signs under, over or inside the letters. The fourth table lists them. They are called points, and the system of points that stands in our Bibles was added to the consonantal text by the Masoretes, long after the books were written. The same system is used for the Aramaic chapters and for the Hebrew ones.

Eight signs mark full vowels: pataḥ, qamets, segol, tsere, ḥiriq, ḥolem and qubbuts, together with shureq, which is a vav with a dot in it. The Tiberian reading makes a difference of length between some of them; the Modern reading does not. Do not memorise the length at this stage: learn to recognise the sign and to give it a sound.

The shewa (two vertical dots under a letter) and the three ḥatef signs are marks of very short vowels or of no vowel. A shewa that begins a word or follows a long vowel is usually pronounced as a very short vowel: the first letter of the word for 'servant' in Daniel 2:4 has one. A shewa between two consonants after a short vowel is usually silent and only closes the syllable: the second shewa in that same word is silent. The three ḥatef signs are a shewa joined to a pataḥ, a segol or a qamets. They are common under alef, he, het and ayin, the letters that cannot easily carry a plain shewa.

sections.heading: The dot inside a letter, and what to ignore for now
body: A dot inside a letter is a dagesh. It has two jobs. In the six letters bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, pe and tav it can show a hard, stop-like sound; without the dot the letter is read in its softer form (bet as v, for example). That is the dagesh in the 'king' of Daniel 2:4, where the dot in the kaf follows a silent shewa. In any letter, a dagesh after a short vowel can instead double the letter: the vav in the last word of Daniel 2:4 is doubled. The rules for deciding are given in grammars; at this stage, watch for the dot and read the word aloud.

Printed Bibles also carry many small signs over and under the words. These are the accents, which show where the stress falls and how the verse is divided. The lessons write Aramaic without them, and you can ignore them for now. A line like the hyphen that joins two words (maqqef) means they are read as one unit.

misunderstandings: Vav is not always v. In the Modern convention it is v; in the Tiberian convention it is w. And when it carries a dot or a dot-vowel it can stand for a vowel (u or o), which A0.1.2 treats.
The points are not part of the oldest consonantal text. A word without points can often be read more than one way. The Masoretes recorded one reading tradition.

The dagesh is not one thing. A dot in bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, pe or tav after a vowel may double the letter; at the start of a syllable it may only harden it. Do not guess from the dot alone: look at the vowel before it.
The Modern and Tiberian columns are not 'right' and 'wrong'. They are two ways to read the same page. Texts and teachers differ.

deeper.heading: Why the same system serves both languages
body: The Masoretes pointed Hebrew and Aramaic parts of the Bible in one system, and in the Aramaic chapters they often had to represent sounds that the system was designed for in Hebrew. Where the points seem to treat an Aramaic word like a Hebrew one, scholars discuss whether they reflect a real Aramaic pronunciation or a reading habit. This course teaches the texts as pointed and does not settle such questions.

rows: Bet has a square bottom corner on the right; kaf is rounded there.
Dalet has a sharp corner at the top right; resh is rounded.
He has a gap between its left stroke and its roof; ḥet is closed; tav has a foot on its left.
Vav is short; final nun runs down below the line.
Zayin has a small bar across the top.
Gimel has a short slanting foot; nun is a plain hook with a flat base.
Samekh is rounded all round; final mem is square.
Ayin is a plain Y; tsade has a small head on its left and a curved tail.
paradigms.note: In the printed Bible the strokes are fine. The difference is small; look at the actual shape.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then spoke the Chaldeans to the king in Aramaic: 'O king, live for ever! tell thy servants the dream, and we will declare the interpretation.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Read the first word from the right: mem, lamed, kaf, alef. The mem has a pataḥ, the lamed has a silent shewa (it closes the first syllable), and the kaf has a dagesh, the dot that follows the silent shewa. The final alef carries no point of its own: the qamets under the kaf is the vowel at the end. The word means 'the king'. The fifth word begins with a het that has a segol; its lamed has a silent shewa; its mem has a qamets; it ends with alef. It means 'the dream'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then spoke the Chaldeans to the king in Aramaic: 'O king, live for ever! tell thy servants the dream, and we will declare the interpretation.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The word for 'servants' begins with a lamed whose shewa is pronounced, as a very short vowel, because it begins the word. The ayin has a pataḥ, the bet has a silent shewa, the dalet has a qamets, and the last letter is a final kaf with a silent shewa. The last word of the verse begins with a nun with a vocal shewa; its vav has a dagesh and a tsere, and the vav is doubled; it ends with alef.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The word for 'image' ends in a mem written in its final form, the closed shape. The tsade carries a shewa and the lamed carries a tsere. The word for 'gold' that follows two words later begins with a dalet that has a shewa, then he with a pataḥ, then a bet at the end of the word without a dagesh. Read it aloud from the right.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The place name Dura starts with a dalet that has a dagesh, followed by a vav with a dot inside it (the shureq, read u), then resh with a qamets and alef. The last word of the verse, Babylon, begins with a bet that has a dagesh and a qamets, then a second bet with a segol, and ends with lamed.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: But if ye declare the dream and the interpretation thereof, ye shall receive of me gifts and rewards and great honour; only declare unto me the dream and the interpretation thereof.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The word for 'before' begins with a qof that carries a ḥatef qamets, the shewa with a qamets, and a very short o. A ḥatef under a letter is a vowel that is shorter than a pataḥ, segol or qamets.

quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: At the right end, moving left.
At the word with the most accents.
At the left end, moving right.
check.explain: The square script runs from right to left. The first word of Daniel 3:1 is the right-most one. The accents help with stress and phrasing but do not tell you where to begin.

check.prompt: In the highlighted word the first bet has a dot inside it and the second has none. How are the two bets read?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The first as v, the second as b.
The first as b, the second as v.
check.explain: A bet with a dagesh is the hard letter, b; a bet without a dagesh is the soft letter, v or a v-like sound. The dot is on the first bet, so it is b, and the second is not.

check.prompt: Which shewa in the highlighted word is pronounced as a very short vowel?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then spoke the Chaldeans to the king in Aramaic: 'O king, live for ever! tell thy servants the dream, and we will declare the interpretation.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The one under the third letter.
The one under the first letter.
The one under the last letter.
check.explain: A shewa under the first letter of a word is vocal, a very short vowel. The shewa under the third letter and the final kaf close their syllables and are silent.

reading.why: Three short verses of plain words, with the final forms, the dagesh, the shewa and every common vowel point. Read them aloud from the right, letter by letter, without trying to translate.
